title: Psoriatic arthritis (psoriasis with joint inflammation)
intro: Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory joint disease that affects some people with psoriasis. It causes pain, swelling and stiffness in joints and tendons, and may damage the joints if untreated. Early diagnosis and treatment can control inflammation and protect joint function.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Symptoms include swollen, painful joints, stiffness especially in the morning that eases with movement, a swollen whole finger or toe known as a sausage digit, heel pain from inflamed tendons, back and neck stiffness and nail changes. Tiredness is common. The pattern varies from a few joints to many, and flare-ups alternate with calmer phases.

sections.heading: Who gets it
paragraphs: Roughly one in five people with psoriasis develops joint involvement, often within years of the skin condition, though joints can be affected first. Risk is higher with severe psoriasis, nail involvement and family history. Genes and immune system overactivity are involved.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Doctors consider symptoms, examine the joints and skin, and use blood tests to check inflammation and rule out other types of arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis. X-rays, ultrasound or MRI detect joint and tendon inflammation and damage. A rheumatologist usually confirms the diagnosis.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Anti-inflammatory painkillers help symptoms. Disease-modifying drugs, such as methotrexate, reduce inflammation and protect joints. If this is not enough, biologic medicines that block specific immune signals, and newer tablets, are effective for both skin and joints. Corticosteroid injections into joints help with local flares. Regular monitoring with blood tests is needed for many of these medicines.

sections.heading: Living with psoriatic arthritis
paragraphs: Exercise, physiotherapy and occupational therapy protect movement and reduce stiffness. Maintaining a healthy weight, stopping smoking and managing stress help. Heart and metabolic health should be checked regularly, since they are affected more often. Support from patient groups can help with the emotional side.

examples.title: Reporting symptoms early
examples.text: Imagine you have psoriasis and notice morning stiffness in your hands. You could note how long it lasts and tell your doctor early, rather than assuming it is ordinary ageing.

examples.title: Staying active
examples.text: Suppose your joints are painful after rest. You might build gentle exercise, such as swimming or cycling, into your day and ask about physiotherapy.
